extracted.intended_audience: railroad companies, municipalities, engineers, attorneys, and applicants seeking federal approval to construct or alter bridges/dams/works over navigable waters of the United States
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing when and how bridges, dams, revetments, and other structures across navigable waters may be authorized, what must be submitted for approval, and the substantive limits (particularly to protect navigation) on approved plans and locations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional authorization for bridges
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no general legislation of Congress authorizing the construction of bridges over streams or waterways whose navigable portions are not wholly within a single State, except as to bridges over the Ohio River; authority has been given by special acts which uniformly contained provisions requiring that the plans of the bridges be submitted to the Secretary of War for approval before construction is commenced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants relying on a Congressional grant must ensure that the special act authorizing the bridge (if required) is complied with, including any plan-submission requirement; examples and citations (various opinions and case references) show practice under special acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: State authorization plus federal approval for intrastate navigable waters
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a stream's navigable extent lies wholly within a single State, bridges 'may be built under authority of the legislature of the State' provided the location and plans are submitted to and approved by the Chief of Engineers and by the Secretary of War before construction is commenced (sec. 7 of 1890 act as amended; sec. 9 of 1899 act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Secretary/Chief review is limited to preventing unreasonable obstructions to navigation; the decision whether a bridge should be built at all is primarily a matter for the State, but approval of plans and location is a federal prerequisite to protect navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approval limited to navigation-protective aspects (scope of review)
rubrics_metrics.description: The jurisdiction of the Secretary of War and of the Chief of Engineers, under the statute, relates to the situation and dimensions of the piers, the length of the spans, width of the draw openings, etc., and is exercised to prevent the structure from being an unreasonable obstruction to navigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secretary may require changes in location/structure to secure free and unobstructed navigation; he will not, under the statute, decide whether a bridge should be built in the abstract — focus is on dimensions and features affecting navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: State authorization is a condition precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The authority of a State for the erection of a bridge over navigable water within the State should be shown as a condition precedent to the approval by the Secretary of War; title to the soil under the water (even if vested in a municipality) does not dispense with the necessity of state authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must provide proper evidence that the State (legislature) has authorized the construction; municipal title is distinct from sovereign authority to grant the franchise or right to build.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and statutory compliance of submitted plans
rubrics_metrics.description: The application for approval must be accompanied by the particulars specified in the act; plans are insufficient as a basis for action where they do not show what the statute requires (e.g., character of structure, full shore line, direction and strength of current, full soundings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maps/plans failing to show statutorily-required details will deprive the Secretary of jurisdiction to approve; in practice some statutory requirements have been treated as directory, but reliance on that is risky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of unreasonable obstructions (cannot stop navigation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislation is to protect navigable waters from unreasonable obstructions; it should not be construed to authorize the location and plan of a bridge which would have the effect of stopping navigation at the point where it is to be constructed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secretary will withhold approval for designs that practically stop navigation; examples include denial where a proposed structure would prevent passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with specific statutory design requirements (draws, locks, spans)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a statutory authorization requires particular features (e.g., a draw of 'not less than' a specified width, or a 'lock or system of locks' in dams), the plans must provide for those features; the Secretary can require reasonably greater dimensions but not unreasonable or impossible ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where statute prescribes minimums (e.g., three channel spans not less than X feet), the Secretary may require greater spans within reasonable limits but cannot require impracticable changes; plans lacking required features (e.g., missing draw) mean no State authority for the proposed plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary's reluctance to approve where special act does not require approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the special act does not require that a plan of the bridge be approved by the Secretary of War, he will preferably not give his approval, because doing so might commit the Government to the sanction of a bridge which might prove to be an obstruction to navigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if approached, the Secretary may decline to approve absent explicit statutory authorization to avoid implicitly validating obstructive structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of corporate identity and acceptance (War Department rule of July 31, 1886)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an act of Congress granting a privilege to a corporation requires Secretary approval of details, the grantee must establish its identity: authenticated copy of charter/articles of incorporation, minutes of organization, extracts showing current officers and acceptance by the company of the provisions and conditions of the act, all properly authenticated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Printed copies certified only by the company's secretary are insufficient; authentication by Secretary of State or proper State official is required. Additional documentary evidence may be required in special cases (e.g., consolidations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specified documentary content accompanying special-act applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the special act designates the kind of bridge, the plan, particulars and specifications required by the statute must accompany the application; otherwise the Secretary has no jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the statute designates details to be submitted, the Secretary may only approve plans that comply exactly; approval of noncomplying plans will be ineffectual and the completed bridge may not be legal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and mandatory time conditions in grants
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative acts that fix times for commencement or completion of construction are generally directory unless made of the essence; where the act makes the time essential, the applicant must show work commenced within the fixed time and the Secretary cannot grant an extension — Congress must.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should verify whether the special act made time of the essence; if so, they must meet statutory deadlines or seek Congressional extension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonassignability of franchise without grantor permission
rubrics_metrics.description: An authority granted by an act of Congress to construct a bridge is a franchise that cannot be assigned without the permission of the grantor (Congress); the Secretary cannot lawfully entertain an application from a party to whom the franchise was transferred without Congressional authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions by construction companies or assignees acting without statutory authorization may be refused; when the bridge exists and the assignee is in actual legal possession, plans for renewal/reconstruction may be accepted from the person in possession (presumption of legality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary's approval power is judicial in nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The power expressly vested in the Secretary by statute to determine whether a bridge is an obstruction to navigation is judicial in nature, not merely ministerial; the statute vests him with specific discretion which pertains to him alone and cannot legally be exercised by an Assistant Secretary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions under this power should be treated as adjudicatory (hearings, discretion), and the Secretary must personally exercise the authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuilding/maintenance rights and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a bridge was constructed under State or Congressional authorization, the right originally given to construct the bridge includes the right to maintain it (repair or rebuild); in reviewing reconstruction plans the Secretary may require changes to secure free and unobstructed navigation and may treat previously fixed statutory minima as potentially subject to increasing requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reconstruction is subject to current navigation-protection standards; the Secretary may condition approval on modifications in location/structural relations to protect navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of temporary works (what counts as a 'bridge')
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain temporary structures (e.g., piles and pontoons placed on ice to be removed before navigation opens) may not be 'bridges' within the meaning of the legislation and thus may be permitted by the Secretary without the same statutory approvals required for bridges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants proposing temporary seasonal structures should seek explicit departmental determination of classification; if not a 'bridge' as defined, standard bridge-approval procedures may not apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal servitude and use of submerged lands for constitutional purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where title to submerged lands is vested in a State, that title is subject to servitudes in favor of navigation and to the right of the United States to use the same for other constitutional purposes (laying mines for harbor defenses, conduits, water mains, etc.), and State statutes cannot be construed to include the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State-granted uses of submerged lands must respect federal navigation and defense servitudes; grantees cannot rely on absolute State title to exclude federal uses.
